The name "anteater" is also commonly applied to the aardvark, numbat, echidnas, and pangolins, although they are not closely related to true anteaters.

Macrocheira kaempferi.text: The Japanese giant spider crab (Macrocheira kaempferi) is a species of marine crab and is the largest crab found in the waters around Japan. At around 3.75 metres (12.3 ft), it has the largest leg-span of any arthropod. The Japanese name for this species is taka-ashi-gani, literally translating to "tall-legged crab". It goes through three main larval stages along with a prezoeal stage to grow to its full size. The Japanese giant spider crab is the sole living member of the genus Macrocheira.

Glaucus atlanticus.text: Glaucus atlanticus (common names include the blue sea dragon, sea swallow, blue angel, blue glaucus, dragon slug, blue dragon, blue sea slug, and blue ocean slug) is a species of sea slug in the family Glaucidae. These sea slugs live in the pelagic zone (open ocean), where they float upside-down by using the surface tension of the water to stay afloat. In addition, they have a gas bubble in their stomach that makes it easier for them to float. They are carried along by the winds and ocean currents.

Lophotrochozoa.text: Lophotrochozoa ("crest/wheel animals") is a clade of protostome animals within the Spiralia. The taxon was established as a monophyletic group based on molecular evidence. The clade includes animals like annelids, molluscs, bryozoans, and brachiopods.

Goliathus goliatus.text: Goliathus goliatus is a very large species of beetle of the family Scarabaeidae, native to tropical Africa. Goliathus goliatus is one of the largest species in the genus Goliathus and one of the largest insects in general, males having a body length of 50–110 millimetres (2.0–4.3 in) and females having a body length of 54–80 millimetres (2.1–3.1 in).

Cyclostomata.text: Cyclostomi, often referred to as Cyclostomata (from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos), meaning "circle", and στόμα (stóma), meaning "mouth", and thus, "circular mouth") is a superclass of vertebrates that comprises the living jawless fish classes: the lampreys and hagfishes. Both groups have jawless mouths with horny epidermal structures that function as teeth called ceratodontes, and branchial arches that are internally positioned instead of external as in the related jawed fishes.

Osteoglossocephalai.text: Osteoglossocephalai is a clade containing all teleosts apart from the Elopiformes, Albulidae (bonefishes), Notacanthiformes, and Anguilliformes (eels).

Paracanthopterygii.text: Paracanthopterygii is a superorder of fishes. Members of this group are called paracanthopterygians. The oldest members are known as fossils from the Cenomanian. It includes three extant orders: Percopsiformes (trout-perches & allies)m Zeiformes (dories), and Gadiformes (cods & allies, including Stylephoriformes).

Brachinus fumans.text: Brachinus fumans, the American bombardier beetle, is a species of ground beetle in the family Carabidae. When disturbed, they eject a hot, noxious chemical spray from their pygidial glands with a popping sound. The spray is produced from a catalyzed reaction between hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide, an aqueous solution of which is stored in the pygidial glands in the beetle's abdomen. Heat from the reaction brings the mixture to near the boiling point of water and produces gas that drives the ejection.

Pseudophyllus titan.text: Pseudophyllus titan, the giant false leaf katydid (a name also used for a few other species), is a species of leaf-mimic bush-cricket of the subfamily Pseudophyllinae found in the canopy of tropical forests in Mainland Southeast Asia, Sindh, Pakistan, Bangladesh (the species' type locality is Sylhet), northeastern India (Assam and Nagaland), and southernmost China (Yunnan). It is among the largest species in the genus Pseudophyllus, which also makes it one of the world's largest Orthoptera, with a typical length of 13 cm from head to tip of the folded wings and a wingspan of 23 cm.

Tettigoniidea.text: Tettigoniidea is an infraorder of the order Orthoptera, with six extant families: Prophalangopsidae (grigs), Anostostomatidae (king crickets or wētā), Cooloola (Cooloola monsters), Gryllacrididae (leaf-rolling or raspy crickets), Stenopelmatidae, and Tettigoniidae (katydids).

Accipitriformes.text: The Accipitriformes (from Latin accipiter 'hawk' and formes 'having the form of') are an order of birds that includes most of the diurnal birds of prey, including hawks, eagles, vultures, kites, ospreys and secretary birds, but not falcons or seriemas. The generally nocturnal owls, also considered birds of prey, are a separate order from the accipitriformes. For a long time, the majority view was to include them with the falcons in the Falconiformes, but many authorities now recognize a separate order Accipitriformes.

Strisores.text: Strisores, sometimes called nightbirds, is a clade of birds that includes the living families and orders Caprimulgidae (nightjars, nighthawks and allies), Nyctibiidae (potoos), Steatornithidae (oilbirds), Podargidae (frogmouths), Apodiformes (swifts and hummingbirds), as well as the Aegotheliformes (owlet-nightjars) whose distinctness was only recently realized. The Apodiformes (which include the "Trochiliformes" of the Sibley–Ahlquist taxonomy) and the Aegotheliformes form the Daedalornithes.

Bathytoshia brevicaudata.text: The short-tail stingray or smooth stingray (Bathytoshia brevicaudata) is a common species of stingray in the family Dasyatidae. It occurs off southern Africa, typically offshore at a depth of 180–480 m (590–1,570 ft), and off southern Australia and New Zealand, from the intertidal zone to a depth of 156 m (512 ft). It is mostly bottom-dwelling in nature and can be found across a range of habitats from estuaries to reefs, but also frequently will swim into open water. One of the largest stingrays in the world, this heavy-bodied species can grow upwards of 2.1 m long.

Imparidentia.text: Imparidentia is a major clade of bivalves named by Bieler, Mikkelsen, and Giribet in 2014; this clade, commonly recovered in phylogenetic analyses, consists of all euheterodonts other than the anomalodesmatans. The name comes from Latin impar "unequal" and dens "tooth", in reference to the unequal hinge teeth seen in members of the clade. The relationships among members of Imparidentia are uncertain.

Strigops habroptilus.text: The kākāpō (Strigops habroptilus), sometimes known as the owl-parrot, is a species of large, nocturnal, ground-dwelling parrot of the superfamily Strigopoidea. It is endemic to New Zealand. Kākāpō can be up to 64 cm (25 in) long. They have a combination of unique traits among parrots: finely blotched yellow–green plumage, a distinct facial disc, owl-like forward-facing eyes with surrounding discs of specially textured feathers, a large grey beak, short legs, large blue feet, relatively short wings and a short tail.

Attacus atlas.text: Attacus atlas, the Atlas moth, is a large saturniid moth endemic to the forests of Asia. The species was described by Carl Linnaeus in his 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae. The Atlas moth is one of the largest lepidopterans, with a wingspan often measuring from 25 to 30 cm. It is only surpassed in wingspan by the white witch (Thysania agrippina) and Attacus caesar, and in wing surface area by the Hercules moth (Coscinocera hercules).

Hydra vulgaris.text: Hydra vulgaris, the fresh-water polyp, is a small freshwater hydroid with length from 10 mm to 30 mm and width about 1 mm. The hydra have four to twelve tentacles that protrude from just outside the mouth. They feed by extending their tentacles and waiting for food to touch the tentacles. They then bring the food to their mouth, ingest and digest the organism. Anything that cannot be digested is egested. Ingestion and egestion occur through the mouth.

Pinnipedia.text: Pinnipeds, commonly known as seals, are a widely distributed and diverse clade of carnivorous, fin-footed, semiaquatic, mostly marine mammals. They comprise the extant families Odobenidae (whose only living member is the walrus), Otariidae (the eared seals: sea lions and fur seals), and Phocidae (the earless seals, or true seals), with 34 extant species and more than 50 extinct species described from fossils. While seals were historically thought to have descended from two ancestral lines, molecular evidence supports them as a monophyletic group (descended from one ancestor).

Aequornithes.text: Aequornithes (from Latin aequor, expanse of water + Greek ornithes, birds), or core water birds, are defined in the PhyloCode as "the least inclusive crown clade containing Pelecanus onocrotalus and Gavia immer", that is, the last common ancestor of the great white pelican and the common loon, as well as its descendants, extinct and extant. Aequornithes, as currently understood, includes the clades Gaviiformes (loons), Sphenisciformes (penguins), Procellariiformes (petrels and albatrosses), Ciconiiformes (storks), Suliformes (gannets and cormorants) and Pelecaniformes (pelicans and herons).

Suliformes.text: The order Suliformes is an order of birds that includes gannets, boobies, frigatebirds, cormorants and darters. The order is recognised by the International Ornithologist's Union. Regarding the recent evidence that the traditional Pelecaniformes is polyphyletic, it has been suggested that the group be divided to reflect the true evolutionary relationships; a 2017 study indicated that they are most closely related to Otidiformes (bustards) and Ciconiiformes (storks).

Tliltocatl vagans.text: Tliltocatl vagans (synonym Brachypelma vagans) is a species of tarantula known commonly as the Mexican red rump. It ranges predominantly in Mexico (including the Yucatán Peninsula), but is also found in Central America. They are terrestrial, burrowing spiders. The reason for the name red rump is because of its distinctive red hairs on its abdomen. Like most tarantulas, they will eat anything they can overpower, which is usually insects, but small lizards and rodents may also be consumed. They can grow to a span of 16.5 cm (6.5 in).

Afrosoricida.text: The clade Afrosoricida (a Latin-Greek compound name which means "looking like African shrews") contains the golden moles of Southern Africa, the otter shrews of equatorial Africa, and the tenrecs of Madagascar. These three groups of small mammals were for most of the 19th and 20th centuries regarded as a part of the Insectivora or Lipotyphla, but both of those groups, as traditionally used, are polyphyletic.

Communostraca.text: The clade Multicrustacea constitutes the largest superclass of crustaceans, containing approximately four-fifths of all described non-hexapod crustacean species, including crabs, lobsters, crayfish, shrimp, krill, prawns, woodlice, barnacles, copepods, amphipods, mantis shrimp and others. The largest branch of Multicrustacea is the class Malacostraca.

Neuropteroidea.text: Neuropteroidea is a clade containing the Neuropterida (snakeflies, alderflies and allies, and lacewings and allies) and Coleopterida (beetles and twisted-wing parasites).

Eupercaria.text: Eupercaria is a subseries of Percomorpha. It contains seven orders: Perciformes (perch-like fish), Centrarchiformes, Labriformes (wrasses, parrotfish, and cales), Acropomatiformes, Acanthuriformes (sturgeonfishes and tangs), Lophiiformes (anglerfish), and Tetraodontiformes (pufferfish and relatives).

Pterophyllum scalare.text: Pterophyllum scalare, most commonly referred to as angelfish or freshwater angelfish, is the most common species of Pterophyllum kept in captivity. It is native to the Amazon Basin in Peru, Colombia, and Brazil. Particularly to the Ucayali river in Peru, the Oyapock River in French Guiana, the Essequibo River in Guyana, the Solimões, the Amapá, and the Amazon rivers in Brazil. It is found in swamps or flooded grounds where vegetation is dense and the water is either clear or silty. Its native waters range from a neutral pH of 7.0 down to near 6.0.

Hieraves.text: Hieraves is a clade of telluravian birds named by Wu et al. (2024) that includes the orders Strigiformes (owls) and Accipitriformes (hawks and their relatives). The Cathartidae (New World vultures) are usually included in Accipitriformes, but some authors treat them as a third order Cathartiformes in the Hieraves. In the past, either owls, New World vultures, and hawks were found to be basal outgroups with respect to Coraciimorphae inside Afroaves, or Accipitriformes and Cathartiformes were recovered as a basal clade in respect to the rest of the members of Telluraves.

Ferae.text: Ferae ('wild beasts') is a mirorder of placental mammals in grandorder Ferungulata, that groups together clades Pan-Carnivora (that includes carnivorans and their fossil relatives, such as hyaenodonts) and Pholidotamorpha (pangolins and their fossil relatives).

Aeluroidea.text: Aeluroidea, Ailuroidea, or Feloidea is the name of a taxon (infraorder or superfamily) comprising cat-like Carnivora. More specifically the taxon comprises: either cat-like Carnivora in the broader sense, i.e. it is synonymous with Feliformia (more specifically either Feliformia sensu stricto, i.e. crown Feliformia, or Feliformia sensu lato, i.e. Pan-Feliformia); or cat-like Carnivora in the narrower sense, i.e. it comprises only the family Felidae (recently also Prionodontidae) and its closest extinct relatives.

Puma lineage.text: The puma lineage is a proposed grouping of the three largest cats in the subfamily Felinae: the cougar, the cheetah, and the jaguarundi. The ancestors of modern cheetahs are thought to have split from the cougar and jaguarundi in the late Miocene, around 6.7 Mya.

Antliophora.text: Antliophora is a clade of insects united by the presence of a spermathecal pump (antlia) in the male reproductive system, comprising the orders Diptera (true flies), Mecoptera (scorpionflies), and Siphonaptera (fleas), with Strepsiptera (twisted-wing parasites) sometimes included. Historically treated as part of the superorder Panorpida (or Mecopterida), the group is supported by both morphological and molecular evidence.

Artiofabula.text: Artiofabula is a major clade of even-toed ungulates (Artiodactyla) that comprises two main living groups: pigs and peccaries (Suina) and the group containing whales, dolphins, hippos, and ruminants (Cetruminantia). The clade was found in molecular phylogenetic analyses and contradicted traditional relationships based on morphological analyses.

Cetruminantia.text: The Cetruminantia are a clade of even-toed ungulated made up of Whippomorpha (hippopotamuses and whales) and their closest living relatives, the Ruminantia (ruminants).

Bovoidea.text: Bovoidea is a superfamily of pecoran ruminants containing the Bovidae (bovids) and Moschidae (musk deer). The Bovoidea today is defined in part by very specific dental and anatomical traits, and genetic research indicates that the Moschidae is the sister taxon to the Bovidae within Pecora.

Passerides.text: Passerides is a clade of birds with global distribution in the order Passeriformes contining much of the diversity of Passeri (songbirds), to the exclusion of the Corvides, Menurides, Climacterides, Meliphagoidea, and Orthonychides.

Passerida.text: Passerida are one of four parvorders contained within the infraorder Passerides. Passerida are omnivorous birds found in East Africa and the Palearctic realm. They live in open areas with minimal trees such as savannas and forest clearings.

Alcoidea.text: Alcoidea is a superfamily of seabirds within the order Charadriiformes. It primarily encompasses the auks (family Alcidae) and related diving seabirds like skuas and jaegers. These birds are highly adapted for a marine lifestyle and are well-known for their diving capabilities, using their wings to 'fly' underwater.

Multicrustacea.text: The clade Multicrustacea constitutes the largest superclass of crustaceans, containing approximately four-fifths of all described non-hexapod crustacean species, including crabs, lobsters, crayfish, shrimp, krill, prawns, woodlice, barnacles, copepods, amphipods, mantis shrimp and others. The largest branch of Multicrustacea is the class Malacostraca.

Pleurodonta.text: Pleurodonta is a clade of iguanas primarily found in the Western Hemisphere, characterized by teeth that are fused to the inner side of the jawbone rather than set in deep sockets. It includes groups such as Anoles (Anolidae), true Iguanas (Iguanidae), Basilisks (Corytophanidae), and Collared Lizards (Crotaphytidae).

Afroinsectivora.text: Afroinsectivora is a mirorder of small, placental mammals native to the African continent and Madagascar. As part of the grandorder Afroinsectiphilia, this clade unites the Afroinsectivores two distinct orders: Macroscelidea (elephant shrews) and Afrosoricida (golden moles, tenrecs, and otter shrews).

Percomorpha.text: Percomorpha is a massive clade of ray-finned fishes that encompasses over 17,000 species, representing nearly half of all living bony fish diversity. This hyper-diverse group includes lineages such as tunas, cichlids, wrasses, seahorses, and flatfishes. Dominating nearly every marine and freshwater ecosystem on Earth, percomorphs underwent a rapid evolutionary radiation following the Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event, resulting in a staggering variety of body shapes, behaviors, and ecological specializations.

Feraequornithes.text: Feraequornithes is a clade of aquatic and marine birds established by moecular data in 2021. It unites five major bird orders: Procellariiformes (albatrosses, petrels), Sphenisciformes (penguins), Ciconiiformes (storks, herons), Suliformes (gannets, cormorants), and Pelecaniformes (pelicans, ibises).

Pelecanes.text: Pelecanes is a clade of Pelecanimorphae consisting of the orders Suliformes (boobies, frigatebirds, darters, and cormorants) and Pelecaniformes (ibises, herons, pelicans, and shoebills).

Otarioidea.text: Otarioidea is a superfamily of pinnipeds that includes the families Odobenidae (the walrus), Otariidae (eared seals or sea lions) and their stem-relatives.

Octopoda.text: An octopus is a soft-bodied, eight-limbed mollusc of the order Octopoda. The order consists of some 300 species and is grouped within the class Cephalopoda with squids, cuttlefish, and nautiloids. Like other cephalopods, an octopus is bilaterally symmetric with two eyes and a beaked mouth at the centre point of the eight limbs. An octopus can radically deform its shape, enabling it to squeeze through small gaps. They trail their appendages behind them as they swim backwards.

Pelecani.text: Pelecani is a suborder of birds in the order Pelecaniformes. It consists of shoebills, hamerkops, pelicans and their extinct relatives. It is likely the sister clade to herons.

Helicina (subordo).text: Helicina is a suborder of land gastropods which consists of former members of the informal group Sigmurethra which were proven to make a clade.

Tetraodontoidei.text: Tetraodontoidei is a suborder of ray-finned fishes, primarily known as puffers, porcupinefishes, and molas. They are united by their fused jaw teeth, which form beak-like plates.

Surniinae.text: Surniinae (small or hawk owls) is a subfamily of the typical owls (Strigidae) first described by French ornithologist Charles Lucien Bonaparte in 1838. It includes ten genera, with the type genus being Surnia.

Muscicapida.text: The Muscicapida is a parvorder of passerine birds within the suborder Passeri. It is a diverse clade, including wrens, mockingbirds, waxwings, and treecreepers amongst others.

Cervini.text: Cervini is a tribe of Old World deer known as 'true' deer. Their internal taxonomy is poorly resolved due to conflict between nuclear DNA and mitochondrial DNA phylogenies.

Striginae.text: Striginae is a major subfamily of the 'true owls' (family Strigidae), comprising numerous genera of predatory, mostly nocturnal birds. Members of this clade are widely distributed across every continent except Antarctica and are physically distinguished by well-developed facial discs used for acoustic location, asymmetrical ear placements, and frequently prominent ear tufts. The subfamily encompasses some of the largest and most familiar owl species, including the eagle-owls, horned owls, and screech owls.

Supramyomorpha.text: Supramyomorpha is a large, diverse clade of rodents established primarily through modern molecular phylogenetic research. It unites several major rodent lineages - specifically the mouse-like rodents (Myomorpha), beaver-like rodents (Castorimorpha), and scaly-tailed squirrels (Anomaluromorpha) - distinguishing them from other major rodent groups like squirrels and porcupines. Representing a vast portion of all living mammal species, members of this infraorder span a wide range of ecological niches, from burrowing pocket gophers to aquatic beavers and cosmopolitan rats.

Arachnopulmonata.text: Arachnopulmonata is a major evolutionary lineage of arachnids defined by the possession of book lungs.. The classification represents a significant consensus in chelicerate phylogenetics, grouping scorpions, spiders, pseudoscorpions, and whip spiders into a single monophyletic group. This clade establishes that land-dwelling arachnids with book lungs share a single, distinct evolutionary origin separate from other arachnid groups like mites and harvestmen.

Ceratomorpha.text: Ceratomorpha is a suborder of odd-toed ungulates (order Perissodactyla) that comprises heavy-bodied, hoofed mammals. Though highly diverse throughout the Cenozoic era with numerous prehistoric lineages, the modern fauna is represented exclusively by two surviving families: the rhinoceroses (Rhinocerotidae) and the tapirs (Tapiridae). Members of this clade are united by specific skeletal characteristics of the skull and feet, distinguishing them from the Hippomorpha, the evolutionary branch that includes modern horses.

Phasiani.text: Phasiani is a major suborder of heavy-bodied, ground-dwelling birds within the order Galliformes (commonly known as landfowl or gamebirds). This diverse group includes some of the most familiar and economically significant birds in the world, such as chickens, turkeys, pheasants, partridges, grouse, guineafowl, and Old and New World quails. Members of Phasiani are distributed globally across nearly every continent and habitat type, ranging from dense tropical rainforests to frozen arctic tundras.

Viverroidea.text: Viverroidea is a clade of feliform carnivorans that includes the family Viverridae (civets and allies) and its sister group, the superfamily Herpestoidea. This superfamily encompasses the remaining modern viverroid families: Herpestidae (mongooses), Eupleridae (Malagasy carnivorans), and Hyaenidae (hyenas and aardwolves). Collectively, the clade comprises a highly diverse array of small to medium-sized mammals primarily native to Africa, southern Europe, and Asia.

Dasyurinae.text: The subfamily Dasyurinae includes several genera of small carnivorous marsupials native to Australia: quolls, kowari, mulgara, kaluta, dibblers, phascogales, pseudantechinuses, and the Tasmanian devil. The subfamily is defined largely on biochemical criteria.

Lemuroidea.text: Lemurs (om Latin lemurēs 'ghosts, spirits of the dead') are wet-nosed primates of the superfamily Lemuroidea, divided into eight families and consisting of 15 genera and around 100 extant species. They are endemic to the island of Madagascar. Most existing lemurs are small, with a pointed snout, large eyes, and a long tail. They usually live in trees and are active at night. Lemurs share resemblance with other primates, but evolved independently from monkeys and apes.

Emydinae.text: Emydinae is a subfamily of freshwater turtles within the family Emydidae, commonly referred to as pond turtles, marsh turtles, or box turtles. The clade is predominantly endemic to the Western Hemisphere, primarily distributed across North America, with the notable exception of the genus Emys, which extends into Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. The subfamily encompasses several prominent living genera, including Terrapene (North American box turtles), Glyptemys (wood and bog turtles), Clemmys (spotted turtles), and Emys (pond turtles).

Delphininae.text: Delphininae is a diverse subfamily of oceanic dolphins within the family Delphinidae, comprising several well-known, highly social marine mammal genera including Tursiops (bottlenose dolphins), Delphinus (common dolphins), and Stenella (spotted and spinner dolphins). Geographically widespread, members of this subfamily are found in temperate, tropical, and subtropical oceans worldwide, with some species specialized for coastal habitats or river systems. They are morphologically distinguished from other delphinids by their well-defined 'beaks' or elongated rostrums.

Agreodontia.text: Agreodontia is an extinct clade of carnivorous marsupials and closely related metatherians that was diverse across Sahul (Australia and New Guinea) from the Oligocene epoch until the late Quaternary. Established to unite specialized meat-eating lineages, the clade includes the modern carnivorous marsupials of the order Dasyuromorphia—such as the extant Tasmanian devil and quolls, alongside the recently extinct thylacine - as well as highly specialized fossil groups like the predatory, bone-cracking marsupial lions of the family Thylacoleonidae and the aberrant bandicoot-like carnivores of Yaralidae.

Himantornithinae.text: Himantornithinae is a subfamily of ground-dwelling birds within the rail family Rallidae. Primarily distributed across Africa, Asia, and Australasia, this newly rearranged group contains a highly diverse assortment of marsh-dwelling and forest birds, ranging from the fully flightless forest rails of New Guinea to wide-ranging wetland species. Members of this clade are generally characterized by their elongated legs and toes adapted for wading through dense, wet vegetation, though their lifestyles vary extensively from secretive, deep-forest foragers to specialized, open-water swimmers.

Fulicini.text: Fulicini is a specialized tribe of aquatic birds within the rail subfamily Himantornithinae, comprising several prominent wetland genera including Fulica (coots), Gallinula (moorhens), and Porzana (crakes). Found on freshwater lakes, marshes, and slow-moving rivers globally, these birds are highly adapted for a swimming and diving lifestyle. They are morphologically distinguished by compressed bodies, short tails, and unique lobed or webbed toes that provide powerful propulsion in water while still allowing agile walking on floating vegetation.

Ursinae.text: Ursinae is a subfamily within the bear family Ursidae that encompasses six living species commonly referred to as the 'true bears', distributed across three genera: Ursus, Helarctos, and Melursus. Widespread throughout the Northern Hemisphere and parts of Southeast Asia, the clade includes well-known species like the brown bear, polar bear, and American black bear, distinct from the giant panda and spectacled bear lineages. Members are anatomically characterized by a robust build, plantigrade posture (walking flat on the soles of their feet), and strong, non-retractable claws well-suited for digging, climbing, and hunting.

Ovis aries.text: Sheep or domestic sheep (Ovis aries) are a domesticated, ruminant mammal typically kept as livestock. Although the term sheep can apply to other species in the genus Ovis, in everyday usage it almost always refers to domesticated sheep. Like all ruminants, sheep are members of the order Artiodactyla, the even-toed ungulates. There are around 1.2 billion domestic sheep as of 2019, making them easily the most common species of sheep.

Presbytini.text: Presbytini is a tribe of Old World monkeys within the subfamily Colobinae, encompassing all the Asian leaf-eating monkeys. Distributed across South and Southeast Asia, this group includes well-known genera such as Presbytis (surilis), Semnopithecus (gray langurs), and the distinct 'odd-nosed' monkeys like the proboscis monkey. Primarily arboreal forest-dwellers, members are anatomically specialized for a folivorous (leaf-based) diet.

Macropodini.text: Macropodini is a diverse tribe of marsupials within the family Macropodidae, containing the true kangaroos, wallabies, and several related lineages. Endemic to Australia and New Guinea, the clade experienced a major evolutionary expansion during the Pliocene epoch as vast grasslands spread across the continent.

Phocini.text: Phocini is a tribe of small to medium-sized earless seals within the subfamily Phocinae, encompassing several prominent northern hemisphere genera including Phoca (harbor and spotted seals), Pusa (ringed, Caspian, and Baikal seals), Halichoerus (gray seal), Pagophilus (harp seal), and Histriophoca (ribbon seal). Primarily distributed throughout Arctic, subpolar, and temperate waters, members of this clade are highly specialized for cold marine environments and are genetically distinguished by a unique 32-chromosome count.

Spirobranchus giganteus.text: Spirobranchus giganteus, commonly known as the Christmas tree worm, is a polychaete worm belonging to the family Serpulidae building calcareous tubes. The S. giganteus lives in coral reefs in the Caribbean. The worms' most distinct features are two 'crowns' shaped like Christmas trees. These are highly modified prostomial palps, which are specialized mouth appendages. Each spiral is composed of feather-like tentacles called radioles, which are heavily ciliated and cause any prey trapped in them to be transported to the worm's mouth.

Astylosternus robustus.text: The hairy frog (Trichobatrachus robustus), also known as the horror frog or Wolverine frog, is a Central African species of frog in the family Arthroleptidae. The hairy frog is notable in possessing retractable 'claws', which it may project through the skin, apparently by intentionally breaking the bones of the toe. When the frog is grabbed or attacked, it breaks a bony nodule near its fingertips and forces the resulting sharpened bones through the skin.

Athesphatanura.text: Athesphatanura is a neotropical clade of hyloid frogs that unites the poison dart frogs of the family Dendrobatidae with their closest relatives in Aromobatidae. Native to Central and South America, members are renowned for their diurnal habits and vibrant, warning coloration. While aromobatids generally lack potent skin toxins, the dendrobatids within this clade are highly toxic, famously sequestering chemical defenses from a specialized diet of ants and mites.

Formicoid.text: The clade formicoid represents the massive lineage containing a large majority of all living ant species across nine subfamilies. This group is evolutionarily distinguished by the development of highly complex eusocial traits, including massive colony sizes, extreme reproductive division of labor, and a remarkable expansion of odorant receptors used for sophisticated chemical communication.

Parasitoida.text: Parasitoida is a highly diverse clade of apocritus wasps within Hymenoptera defined by their specialized parasitic lifestyle. These insects reproduce by laying their eggs inside or on other arthropod hosts, which the developing larvae eventually consume and kill. Many lineages within this group have evolved extraordinary biological adaptations, including the domestication of ancient viral genes to manipulate and suppress host immune systems.

Poecilophysidea.text: Poecilophysidea is a resurrected arachnid clade that unites camel spiders (Solifugae) and acariform mites (Acariformes) based on recent phylogenomic evidence. Morphologically, members of this group share a highly unique division of the front body known as a sejugal furrow, which structurally separates the second and third pairs of walking legs.

Passeroidea.text: Passeroidea is the largest superfamily of songbirds, encompassing over 1,500 species across more than 20 diverse families. This globally distributed radiation includes familiar groups like sparrows, finches, weavers, and New World warblers. They are primarily small-bodied, perching birds characterized by melodious songs, complex plumages, and varied diets that often focus on seeds, nectar, or insects.

Panscorpiones.text: Panscorpiones is a newly established clade of arachnids that unites scorpions (Scorpiones) and pseudoscorpions (Pseudoscorpiones) as sister groups. Discovered through advanced genomic sampling, this grouping refutes traditional physical classifications. Despite massive differences in size and the presence of a stinging tail in true scorpions, both lineages share predatory lifestyles and heavily modified, pincer-like front appendages.

Agastorophrynia.text: Agastorophrynia is a large clade of hyloid frogs that encompasses true toads (Bufonidae) and the species-rich superfamily of poison dart frogs and their allies (Dendrobatoidea). Originally proposed during large-scale molecular reclassifications of amphibians, this grouping highlights the deep genetic relationship between the rough-skinned, terrestrial toads and the toxic, diurnal dart frogs of the New World tropics.

Allodapanura.text: Allodapanura is a clade of ranoid frogs, sister to Natatanura. It contains Microhylidae (the narrow-mouthed frogs) and Afrobatrachia (representing more than half of the diversity of African frogs).

Leopard cat lineage.text: The leopard cat lineage is an evolutionary branch of small wild cats native to Asia that includes the genera Prionailurus and Otocolobus. Diverging from other felids during the late Miocene, this group contains highly distinct species like the fishing cat, flat-headed cat, and Pallas's cat.

Cephenemyia stimulator.text: Cephenemyia stimulator, commonly known as the roe deer botfly, is a parasitic fly widespread across the Palearctic realm of Europe. Belonging to the family Oestridae, this large, bee-mimicking fly relies on the roe deer (Capreolus capreolus) as its primary host. Females reproduce viviparously, directly ejecting larvae into the deer’s nostrils, which then migrate to mature within the pharyngeal and nasal cavities - a myiasis that frequently causes severe respiratory distress, secondary infections, or even suffocation in heavily infested animals.
